column5: This dataset provides modeled estimates of 1 month hydrological fluxes at a 0.25-degree resolution over Alaska and Canada for the years 1979-2018. These estimates were generated using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) macroscale hydrological model version 4.1.2, which includes water and energy balance schemes, and operates at a 0.25-degree spatial and 1 day temporal resolution over the 38-year period. The gridded output data products are 1 month averages of water balance variables, including precipitation (P), evapotranspiration (E), 'P minus E', evaporation, soil moisture in three soil layers, base flow and runoff, snow depth, snow water equivalent (SWE), and snow sublimation. Additionally, energy balance variables are included, such as surface temperature, albedo, latent and sensible heat flux, ground heat flux, and short- and long-wave radiative fluxes. The dataset also aggregates 1 day modeled values for precipitation and evapotranspiration to water years, and provides a 30-year climate normal average for precipitation.

column5: The 1 month climatology dataset contains a series of land surface parameters simulated from the Noah 3.6.1 model in the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS). The dataset comprises of 12 1 month files, each representing the 1 month data averaged over 35 years from 1982 to 2016, based on the FLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 Global 1 month 0.1 x 0.1 degree (MERRA-2 and CHIRPS) V001 (FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M_001) 1 month data. The data are in 0.10 degree resolution and the spatial coverage is global (60S, 180W, 90N, 180E). The FLDAS regional 1 month climatology datasets will no longer be available and have been superseded by the global 1 month climatology dataset. More information about the 1 month FLDAS can be found from the dataset landing page for FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M_001 and the FLDAS README document. In November 2020, all FLDAS data were post-processed with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, some grid boxes over inland water were considered as over land and, thus, had non-missing values. The post-processing corrected this issue and masked out all model output data over inland water; the post-processing did not affect the meteorological forcing variables. More information on this can be found in the FLDAS README document, and the MOD44W MODIS land mask is available on the FLDAS Project site. If you had downloaded any FLDAS data prior to November 2020, please download the data again to receive the post-processed data.

column5: The NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2 (GLDAS-2) comprises three distinct components: GLDAS-2.0, GLDAS-2.1, and GLDAS-2.2, each serving specific purposes within the system. GLDAS-2.0, extending from 1948 to 2014, relies solely on Princeton meteorological forcing input data, ensuring temporal consistency throughout the dataset. GLDAS-2.1, operational from 2000 to the present, incorporates a blend of model and observational data, offering a comprehensive approach to land surface data assimilation. GLDAS-2.2 introduces a new paradigm by incorporating data assimilation (DA) techniques. Unlike its predecessors, GLDAS-2.2 harnesses the power of assimilating data from various sources, leading to enhanced accuracy in its outputs. The specifics of forcing data, DA observation sources, variables, and schemes employed vary across different GLDAS-2.2 products. This data set, GLDAS-2.0 1 month 1.0 degree, contains a series of land surface variables generated through temporal averaging of GLDAS-2.0 3-1 hours data simulated from the Catchment Land Surface Model 3.6 in Land Information System (LIS) Version 7. The data set currently cover from January 1948 to December 2014, but will be extended as the forcing data becomes available. The GLDAS-2.0 data are archived and distributed in NetCDF format. The GLDAS-2.0 model simulations were initialized on January 1, 1948, using soil moisture and other state fields from the LSM climatology for that day of the year. The simulations were forced by the global meteorological forcing data set from Princeton University (Sheffield et al., 2006). Each simulation uses the common GLDAS data sets for land water mask (MOD44W: Carroll et al., 2009) and elevation (GTOPO30) along with the model default land cover and soils datasets. Catchment model uses the Mosaic land cover classification and soils, topographic, and other model-specific parameters were derived in a consistent manner as in the NASA/GMAO?s GEOS-5 climate modeling system. The MODIS based land surface parameters are used in the current GLDAS-2.0 and GLDAS-2.1 products. In October 2020, all 3-1 hours and 1 month GLDAS-2 data were post-processed with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, some grid boxes over inland water were considered as over land and, thus, had non-missing values. The post-processing corrected this issue and masked out all model output data over inland water; the post-processing did not affect the meteorological forcing variables. More information can be found in the GLDAS-2 README. The MOD44W MODIS land mask is available on the GLDAS Project site.

column5: This product serves as a comprehensive compilation of multi-variate data, designed to harmonize the varying scales of numerous measurements sourced from diverse resources. It amalgamates and maps these measurements to provide a detailed depiction of near-surface atmospheric properties alongside variations in land surface characteristics spanning from diurnal to decadal time scales. Given the sparsity or incompleteness of many data products, particularly those derived from surface measurements, procedures have been devised to address missing values. The data product comprises a series of 1 day global files, where quantities are mapped onto a 1.0-degree equivalent equal-area grid. Time sampling is reported at either 1 day intervals or every three hour. The temporal coverage of these products spans a decade, from 1998 to 2007, allowing for an extensive examination of environmental dynamics over this period.

column5: The National Climate Assessment - Land Data Assimilation System (NCA-LDAS) is a critical component supporting the activities of the United States Global Change Research Program's NCA. It offers high-resolution, gridded, 1 day time series data products, focusing on terrestrial water and energy balance stores, states, and fluxes across the continental U.S. These datasets are derived from land surface hydrologic modeling with multivariate assimilation of satellite Environmental Data Records (EDRs). The primary aim is to deliver top-tier terrestrial hydrology products to enhance scientific comprehension, adaptation, and management of water and energy resources amidst a changing climate. NCA-LDAS version 2.0 spans the satellite era from January 1979 to December 2016, focusing on the continental United States. At its core, NCA-LDAS utilizes multivariate assimilation techniques to integrate historical and contemporary satellite-based data records within the Noah Version 3.3 land-surface model (LSM) at a resolution of 1/8th degree. This integration is facilitated through NASA's Land Information System (LIS) software framework. The data are provided at a 1 day temporal resolution. It's important to note that NCA-LDAS V001 data will no longer be accessible, having been replaced by V2.0. NCA-LDAS encompasses 42 variables, including land-surface fluxes (such as precipitation, radiation, and latent and sensible heat), stores (including soil moisture and snow), states (such as surface temperature), and routing variables (like runoff, streamflow, and flooded area). These variables are driven by atmospheric forcing data from the North American Land Data Assimilation System Phase 2 (NLDAS-2). NCA-LDAS extends the capabilities of NLDAS by incorporating multivariate assimilation of earth observations, including soil moisture, snow, and irrigation. EDRs assimilated into NCA-LDAS encompass soil moisture and snow depth primarily from microwave sensors such as SMMR, SSM/I, AMSR-E, ASCAT, AMSR-2, SMOS, and SMAP, irrigation intensity estimates from MODIS, and snow-covered area from MODIS and the multisensor IMS snow product.

column5: The National Climate Assessment - Land Data Assimilation System (NCA-LDAS) is a system designed to analyze terrestrial water dynamics to support the activities of the United States Global Change Research Program's National Climate Assessment (NCA). It provides gridded, 1 day data on terrestrial water and energy balances across the continental U.S. These data are derived from hydrological modeling and assimilation of satellite Environmental Data Records (EDRs), aimed at enhancing scientific understanding, adaptation, and management of water and energy resources amidst changing climate conditions. This dataset encompasses historical trends in terrestrial hydrology across the contiguous United States for the water years spanning 1980-2015, obtained through 1 day reanalysis by NCA-LDAS. Utilizing the uncoupled Noah version 3.3 land surface model (LSM) at 1/8th degree resolution, the system is driven by NLDAS-2 meteorological data, rescaled Climate Prediction Center precipitation, and assimilated satellite-derived soil moisture, snow depth, and irrigation data. Annual hydrological indicators' trends are assessed using the nonparametric Mann-Kendall test, with significance set at p < 0.1. Additionally, a precipitation trend field (annual total) is provided for comparison purposes, without undergoing significance testing.

column5: This data set from the ISLSCP Initiative II includes near-surface meteorological variables, surface heat, moisture, and momentum fluxes, as well as land surface state variables. The spatial resolution is 1 degree in both latitude and longitude. The data are categorized into four temporal groups: fixed fields (time-invariant and 1 month mean annual cycle), 1 month mean fields, 1 month 3-1 hours diurnal fields, and 3-1 hours fields. The Center for Ocean-Land Atmosphere Studies (COLA) near-surface data set for ISLSCP II was derived from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP)/Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Model Inter-comparison Project (AMIP-II) reanalysis. This reanalysis covers the years 1979 to 2003, while the ISLSCP II data set specifically spans from 1986 to 1995. The reanalysis aimed to improve upon the original NCEP/National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) reanalysis for General Circulation Model (GCM) validation. To align the NCEP/DOE reanalysis with the ISLSCP 1-degree grid, the data set was regridded from its native T62 Gaussian grid resolution (192 x 94 grid boxes globally) to the required 1-degree resolution. There are 136 compressed (.tar.gz) data files in this data set, with each file containing data in ASCII (.asc) format when uncompressed.

column5: The Oregon Transect Ecosystem Research (OTTER) Project was a collaborative initiative between NASA and multiple universities aimed at understanding the ecology of western coniferous forests by leveraging remote sensing technology alongside ground observations. OTTER, being interdisciplinary in nature, focused on testing a model designed to estimate the major fluxes of carbon, nitrogen, and water within a temperate coniferous forest ecosystem. Six distinct sites in Oregon, spanning varied elevational and climatic gradients, were selected for intensive study. The transect originated at Cascade Head on the Pacific coast, traversed the outskirts of Corvallis, continued through dense Douglas fir forests in Scio, proceeded through a mountain hemlock/subalpine fir community at Santiam Pass, passed a Ponderosa pine community near Metolius, and concluded at Juniper, located east of Sisters. In total, the transect spanned approximately 300 kilometers from west to east. The project's objectives included simulating and predicting ecosystem processes such as photosynthesis, transpiration, above-ground production, nitrogen transformation, respiration, decomposition, and hydrologic processes. To achieve these goals, a combination of field, laboratory, and remote sensing techniques were employed to estimate key vegetation and environmental parameters. column5: This dataset offers gridded modeled hydrological time series, driven by medium- to sub-seasonal range meteorological reforecasts, providing a consistent representation of key hydrological variables across the European Flood Awareness System (EFAS) domain. Covering 20 years of sub-1 day reforecasts, initialized twice weekly (Mondays and Thursdays), the dataset includes: River discharge, Soil moisture for three soil layers, and Snow water equivalent. Auxiliary (time-invariant) data are also provided to aid the interpretation of river discharge and soil moisture data. These include upstream area, elevation, soil depth, wilting capacity, and field capacity, with the latter three specified for each of the three soil layers in LISFLOOD. The dataset was generated by forcing the open-source LISFLOOD hydrological model at a 1x1 arcminute resolution (~1.5 km at EFAS latitudes) with ensemble meteorological reforecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). In version 4.0, the LISFLOOD model was applied at a 5x5 km resolution. Reforecasts, which are historical forecasts used to evaluate forecast system skill or develop statistical error correction tools, are initialized twice weekly with lead times up to 46 days, at 6-1 hours intervals over 20 years. For detailed information on the reforecast dataset production, refer to the documentation. Companion datasets available through the Climate Data Store (CDS) include operational forecasts, historical simulations for deriving hydrological climatology, and seasonal forecasts and reforecasts for long-term forecasting needs. For global hydrological data, refer to the Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS) forecasts and historical simulations.

column4: UERRA regional reanalysis for Europe on soil levels from 1961 to 2019
column5: The UERRA dataset provides climate estimations for Europe by integrating model data with observations through the UERRA-HARMONIE and MESCAN-SURFEX systems. UERRA-HARMONIE is a three-dimensional data assimilation system, while MESCAN-SURFEX is a complementary surface analysis system. These assimilation systems can identify biases between observations and filter high-quality data from poor data. The principles of physics enable them to generate estimates in areas with sparse data coverage. Reanalysis is highly valuable due to its consistent format, offering estimates at each grid point in Europe at regular intervals over extended periods. SURFEX, the land surface Platform/Project, is driven by downscaled forecast fields from UERRA-HARMONIE and MESCAN analyses. It operates offline, without feedback to the atmospheric analysis from MESCAN or the UERRA-HARMONIE data assimilation cycles. Although the observing system has evolved significantly over time, with initially sparse networks impacting analysis quality, the assimilation system can mitigate data gaps. The UERRA dataset surpasses global reanalysis products in accuracy due to its higher horizontal resolution, capturing more regional details like topography and utilizing dense observation networks more effectively.

column5: This dataset offers 1 day historical outputs from a Water Balance Model based on a Thornthwaite-type, single bucket model. The model utilizes climate inputs from GridMet 1 day temperature and precipitation data for the Continental United States (CONUS). Key output variables from the Water Balance Model include Potential Evapotranspiration (PET, mm), Actual Evapotranspiration (AET, mm), Moisture Deficit (Deficit, mm), Soil Water content (soilwater, mm), Runoff (mm), Rainfall (mm), and Accumulated Snow Water Equivalent (accumswe, mm). The dataset spans from January 1 to December 31 for the years 1980 through 2021 for the CONUS region. Each Water Balance Model variable is provided as separate files, organized by variable and year, with a spatial resolution of 1 km x 1 km and a 1 day temporal resolution. The data are presented in a North America Lambert Conformal Conic projection and are formatted in accordance with the standardized Climate and Forecast (CF)-compliant NetCDF file format.

column5: BasinATLAS, a component of the HydroATLAS database within HydroSHEDS, offers a standardized collection of hydro-environmental attribute information for watersheds worldwide at high spatial resolution. This dataset covers 56 variables, partitioned into 281 attributes across six categories: hydrology, physiography, climate, land cover & use, soils & geology, and anthropogenic influences.The watersheds are categorized from level 1 (coarse) to level 12 (detailed) using Pfafstetter coding. The watershed delineation is based on the NASA SRTM Digital Elevation Map (DEM) for latitudes below 60°N and the USGS HYDRO1k DEM for regions above 60°N. It's important to note that the quality of HydroATLAS data is lower for regions above 60°N latitude, due to the absence of SRTM elevation data and reliance on the coarser-resolution HYDRO1k DEM provided by the USGS. HydroSHEDS was developed by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) Conservation Science Program in collaboration with the U.S. Geological Survey, the International Centre for Tropical Agriculture, The Nature Conservancy, and the Center for Environmental Systems Research at the University of Kassel, Germany.

column4: CERRA-Land sub-1 day regional reanalysis data for Europe from 1984 to present
column5: The Copernicus European Regional ReAnalysis Land (CERRA-Land) dataset provides high-resolution, spatially, and temporally consistent historical reconstructions of surface and soil variables. This dataset meets the increasing demand for detailed precipitation and surface data, which are essential for water resource management and climate change impact studies. CERRA-Land is part of a regional surface reanalysis approach that reconstructs past surface variables using advanced models over several decades. Reanalysis combines model data with observations to create a complete and consistent dataset by using data assimilation, a method where previous forecasts are optimally combined with newly available observations to produce updated estimates of atmospheric states. Unlike numerical weather prediction, reanalysis can take more time to incorporate historical observations, improving the quality of the dataset. The soil is discretized into 14 layers to solve heat and water transfer equations, and the system includes a surface precipitation analysis and a 12-layer snow model, enhancing snowpack representation over Europe compared to the CERRA dataset. This dataset consistently tracks the evolution of soil moisture, soil temperature, and snowpack over several decades at higher resolution than ERA5 and ERA5-Land, making it particularly useful for water resource management and climate change studies. The enhanced horizontal resolution of CERRA-Land allows for a better description of model topography and physiographic data compared to global reanalysis products.

column5: This data set, part of the ISLSCP Initiative II data collection, provides meteorological data at various temporal resolutions: fixed, 1 month, 1 month-6-1 hours, 6-1 hours, and 3-1 hours. The data were derived from the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) near-surface meteorology data set, specifically the 40-year re-analysis known as ERA-40 (Simmons and Gibson, 2000), which covers the period from 1957 to 2001. The data were processed onto the ISLSCP II Earth grid, featuring a spatial resolution of 1-degree in both latitude and longitude, and span the common ISLSCP II period from 1986 to 1995. The ECMWF forecast system, called the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS), was developed in cooperation with Meteo-France. For ERA-40, IFS is used with 60 levels ranging from the top of the model at 10 Pa to the lowest level at approximately 10 meters above the surface. There are 46 compressed (.tar.gz) data files in this data set. Each uncompressed file contains space-delimited text (.asc) data files.

column5: The Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS), developed at Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) and funded by the NASA Western Water Applications Office, provides water managers and stakeholders in the western United States with a long-term record of near-surface hydrology for use in drought assessment and water resources planning. WLDAS leverages advanced capabilities in land surface modeling and data assimilation to furnish a system that is customized for stakeholders? needs in the region. WLDAS uses NASA?s Land Information System (LIS) to configure and drive the Noah Multiparameterization (Noah-MP) Land Surface Model (LSM) version 3.6 to simulate land surface states and fluxes. WLDAS uses meteorological observables from the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2) including precipitation, incoming shortwave and longwave radiation, near surface air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and surface pressure along with parameters such as vegetation class, soil texture, and elevation as inputs to a model that simulates land surface energy and water budget processes. Outputs of the model include soil moisture, snow depth and snow water equivalent, evapotranspiration, soil temperature, as well as derived quantities such as groundwater recharge and anomalies of the state variables.

column4: CERRA sub-1 day regional reanalysis data for Europe on single levels from 1984 to present
column5: The Copernicus European Regional ReAnalysis (CERRA) datasets provide spatially and temporally consistent historical reconstructions of meteorological variables both in the atmosphere and at the surface. These datasets are divided into four subsets: single levels (atmospheric and surface quantities), height levels (upper-air fields up to 500m), pressure levels (upper-air fields up to 1hPa), and model levels (native levels of the model). This specific entry offers reanalysis and forecast data on single levels for Europe from 1984 to the present. Common atmospheric parameters included in both reanalysis and forecast data are temperature and wind, while others like 10m wind gust and radiative fluxes are exclusively produced by the forecast model. Reanalysis merges model data with observations using the laws of physics to form a comprehensive and consistent dataset. This process, known as data assimilation, is similar to methods used by numerical weather prediction centers, where previous forecasts are combined with new observations to produce updated estimates of atmospheric states, known as analyses. Unlike numerical weather predictions, reanalysis operates at a reduced resolution, enabling the creation of datasets spanning several decades. Reanalysis benefits from not having the urgency of issuing timely forecasts, allowing for the collection of more observations and the incorporation of improved, reprocessed historical observations, enhancing the quality of the reanalysis product. The CERRA dataset was produced using the HARMONIE-ALADIN limited-area numerical weather prediction and data assimilation system, referred to as the CERRA system. This system employs a three-dimensional variational data assimilation scheme for the atmospheric state at each assimilation time. The CERRA reanalysis provides atmospheric estimates at each model grid point over Europe at regular intervals, using a consistent data format over a long period. Inputs to the CERRA reanalysis include observational data, lateral boundary conditions from the ERA5 global reanalysis as prior estimates of the atmospheric state, and physiographic datasets describing the surface characteristics. The observing system has evolved over time, and although the data assimilation system can resolve data gaps, the sparser observational networks of past periods (such as the limited satellite data in the 1980s) can impact the accuracy of analyses. Uncertainty estimates for reanalysis variables are provided by the CERRA-EDA, a 10-member ensemble data assimilation system. The CERRA data is expected to add value over global reanalysis products through its higher horizontal resolution, allowing for a better description of model topography and physiographic data, and the assimilation of more surface observations.

column5: The Vegetation/Ecosystem Modeling and Analysis Project (VEMAP) was a multi-institutional, international effort that addressed the response of biogeography and biogeochemistry to environmental variability in climate and other drivers in both space and time domains. The objectives of VEMAP were to study the intercomparing of biogeochemistry models and vegetation type distribution models (biogeography models) and determine their sensitivity to changing climate, elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations, and other sources of altered forcing. Soil properties were based on a 10-km gridded EPA soil database developed by Kern (1994, 1995). Two soil coverages are provided in the Kern data set: one from the USDA Soil Conservation Service (SCS) national soil database (NATSGO) and the other from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization soil database (FAO 1974- 78). Only the SCS NATSGO soils are included in the VEMAP set. Physical consistency in soils data was incorporated by representing a grid cell's soil by a set of dominant (modal) soil profiles, rather than by a simple average of soil properties. Because soil processes, such as soil organic matter turnover and water balance, are non-linearly related to soil texture and other soil parameters, simulations based on dominant soil profiles and their frequency distribution can account for soil dynamics that would be lost if averaged soil properties were used. To spatially aggregate Kern data to the 0.5 degree grid, we used cluster analysis to group the sub-grid 10-km elements into up to 4 modal soil categories (Kittel et al. 1995). In this statistical approach, cell soil properties are represented by the set of modal soils, rather than by an \average soil.\" We also provide cell- averaged soil data."

column5: The NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2 (GLDAS-2) comprises three distinct components: GLDAS-2.0, GLDAS-2.1, and GLDAS-2.2, each serving specific purposes within the system. GLDAS-2.0, extending from 1948 to 2014, relies solely on Princeton meteorological forcing input data, ensuring temporal consistency throughout the dataset. GLDAS-2.1, operational from 2000 to the present, incorporates a blend of model and observational data, offering a comprehensive approach to land surface data assimilation. GLDAS-2.2 introduces a new paradigm by incorporating data assimilation (DA) techniques. Unlike its predecessors, GLDAS-2.2 harnesses the power of assimilating data from various sources, leading to enhanced accuracy in its outputs. The specifics of forcing data, DA observation sources, variables, and schemes employed vary across different GLDAS-2.2 products. The GLDAS-2.0 model simulations commence on January 1, 1948, with initialization utilizing soil moisture and other state fields sourced from the LSM climatology corresponding to that specific day of the year. These simulations are driven by the global meteorological forcing dataset developed by Princeton University. Each simulation integrates common GLDAS datasets for land-water mask (MOD44W: Carroll et al., 2009) and elevation (GTOPO30), alongside default land cover and soil datasets inherent to the model. The Catchment model adopts the Mosaic land cover classification and soil parameters derived consistently with the NASA/GMAO?s GEOS-5 climate modeling system. The current GLDAS-2.0 and GLDAS-2.1 products leverage MODIS-based land surface parameters. The resulting GLDAS-2.0 data is archived and disseminated in NetCDF format, facilitating accessibility and compatibility across a wide range of Platform/Projects and applications.

column5: The NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2 (GLDAS-2) comprises three distinct components: GLDAS-2.0, GLDAS-2.1, and GLDAS-2.2, each serving specific purposes within the system. GLDAS-2.0, extending from 1948 to 2014, relies solely on Princeton meteorological forcing input data, ensuring temporal consistency throughout the dataset. GLDAS-2.1, operational from 2000 to the present, incorporates a blend of model and observational data, offering a comprehensive approach to land surface data assimilation. GLDAS-2.2 introduces a new paradigm by incorporating data assimilation (DA) techniques. Unlike its predecessors, GLDAS-2.2 harnesses the power of assimilating data from various sources, leading to enhanced accuracy in its outputs. The specifics of forcing data, DA observation sources, variables, and schemes employed vary across different GLDAS-2.2 products. The GLDAS-2.0 1.0-degree 3-1 hours dataset contains simulated land surface variables derived from the Catchment Land Surface Model 3.6 within the Land Information System (LIS) Version 7 framework. This dataset currently covers the period from January 1948 to December 2014, with plans for extension as additional forcing data becomes available. The GLDAS-2.0 data is archived and distributed in NetCDF format. Initialization of GLDAS-2.0 model simulations on January 1, 1948, utilizes soil moisture and other state fields from the LSM climatology for that specific day. Simulations are forced by the global meteorological forcing dataset from Princeton University. Each simulation incorporates common GLDAS datasets for land-water mask (MOD44W: Carroll et al., 2009) and elevation (GTOPO30), along with default land cover and soil datasets. The Catchment model adopts the Mosaic land cover classification, with topographic and other model-specific parameters derived in a manner consistent with the NASA/GMAO?s GEOS-5 climate modeling system. MODIS-based land surface parameters are utilized in both GLDAS-2.0 and GLDAS-2.1 products. In October 2020, all 3-1 hours and 1 month GLDAS-2 data underwent post-processing with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. This post-processing rectified issues where some grid boxes over inland water were erroneously considered as over land, resulting in non-missing values. The post-processing corrected this by masking out all model output data over inland water, without affecting the meteorological forcing variables. Additional details can be found in the GLDAS-2 README. The MOD44W MODIS land mask is available on the GLDAS Project site. If data was downloaded prior to November 2020, it is recommended to re-download the data to receive the post-processed version.

column5: This 1 month climatology data set contains a series of land surface parameters simulated from the Mosaic land-surface model (LSM) for Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2). The data are in 1/8th degree grid spacing. The temporal resolution is 1 month, ranging from January to December. The NLDAS-2 1 month climatology data are the 1 month data averaged over the thirty years (1980 - 2009) of the NLDAS-2 1 month data. The file format is WMO GRIB-1. A brief description about the NLDAS-2 1 hours and 1 month Mosaic LSM data can be found from the GCMD DIFs for GES_DISC_NLDAS_MOS0125_H_V002 and GES_DISC_NLDAS_MOS0125_M_V002. Details about the NLDAS-2 configuration of the Mosaic LSM can be found in Xia et al. (2012). The NLDAS-2 Mosaic model 1 month climatology data set contains thirty-seven fields. The data set applies a user-defined parameter table to indicate the contents and parameter number. The GRIBTAB file shows a list of parameters for this data set, along with their Product Definition Section (PDS) IDs and units

column5: This dataset offers 1 month historical outputs from a Water Balance Model based on a Thornthwaite-type, single bucket model. The model utilizes climate inputs from GridMet 1 day temperature and precipitation data for the Continental United States (CONUS). Key output variables from the Water Balance Model include Potential Evapotranspiration (PET, mm), Actual Evapotranspiration (AET, mm), Moisture Deficit (Deficit, mm), Soil Water content (soilwater, mm), Runoff (mm), Rainfall (mm), and Accumulated Snow Water Equivalent (accumswe, mm). The dataset spans from January 1 to December 31 for the years 1980 through 2021 for the CONUS region. Each Water Balance Model variable is provided as separate files, organized by variable and year, with a spatial resolution of 1 km x 1 km and a 1 day temporal resolution. The data are presented in a North America Lambert Conformal Conic projection and are formatted in accordance with the standardized Climate and Forecast (CF)-compliant NetCDF file format.

column5: An analysis of spatial and temporal drought patterns in moist tropical forests, along with their correlation to forest fire regimes, was conducted from 1995 to 2001 using a simple GIS soil-water balance model called RisQue (Risco de Queimadasa -- Fire Risk) in the Amazon Basin. The provided data includes model output estimates of maximum plant-available soil water (PAWmax) at a depth of 10 meters, along with model data inputs of 1 month precipitation and evapotranspiration, all at an 8-kilometer resolution. RisQue calculates PAWmax at 10 meters by initially creating a map of PAWmax at a depth of 1-2 meters, which is developed using 1,565 RADAMBRASIL soil texture profiles and empirical relationships between soil texture and critical soil water parameters. This map is then interpolated to an 8-kilometer resolution. In RisQue, plant-available soil water (PAW) undergoes depletion due to 1 month evapotranspiration, estimated using the Penman Monteith equation and satellite-derived radiation, and is recharged by 1 month precipitation. The dataset includes three types of files: two compressed (*.zip) files containing 83 files of evapotranspiration data and 89 files of precipitation data in ASCII grid format, and one GeoTIFF image (.tif) representing the map of maximum percent available water at a 10-meter depth, predicted over the period 1995-2001. All files in this dataset adhere to the standard arc/info ASCII grid format and have an 8-kilometer resolution.
